name: Zimbabwe
sources: GDP $8.8bn and 10.2m people (World Bank, 1990). Per head this is roughly twice Kenya's and the second-most industrialised economy in sub-Saharan Africa, a legacy of the UDI sanctions years forcing import substitution.

Inflation 17.4% in 1990 (Central Statistical Office CPI); Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe bank rate around 14%, so real rates were negative under a comprehensive exchange-control and price-control regime. The Economic Structural Adjustment Programme that dismantled it was announced in 1990 and began in 1991.

Tax take 32% of GDP, by far the highest in this region and comparable to a European state: an inherited Rhodesian revenue administration collecting from a formal-sector economy with real corporate taxpayers.

Defence 4.5% of GDP: roughly 50,000 in the ZDF, including the brigade-strength deployment guarding the Beira corridor in Mozambique against RENAMO, which ran from 1985 to 1993 and at its peak was around 10,000 men outside the country.

Stability 58 and authoritarianism 0.60: the 28-30 March 1990 general election gave ZANU-PF 117 of 120 elected seats. Mugabe put a one-party state to the ZANU-PF central committee in August 1990 and it was rejected; the state of emergency in force since 1965 finally lapsed in July 1990.
Separatism 0.10: Matabeleland and the ZAPU question, largely settled by the 22 December 1987 Unity Accord that merged ZAPU into ZANU-PF after the Gukurahundi campaign of 1983-87. Low, but not zero.
Military strength 5: an experienced force with T-54/55s, Hawk trainers used as light strike and the only African army of the period with a sustained cross-border deployment, but no lift of its own.
